author: STAFF REPORTS
title: New 3D-printing techniques improve safety for energetic material - NewsBreak
text:
By STAFF REPORTS ,
5 hours ago Energetic materials manufacturing, which includes explosives, pyrotechnics, and propellants, requires precise formulations, conditions, and procedures to ensure their intended performance and levels of safety.
Due to the fact that any minor environmental shift can dramatically alter the functionality of these materials, Monique McClain, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering, is developing advanced methods to control these materials’ behaviors throughout the manufacturing process, down to the particle level.
McClain specializes in the “upstream” or earlier manufacturing stages, analyzing how manufacturing alters the structure and mechanical properties of an energetic material, as well as how these changes affect performance and sensitivity.
“An energetic material’s manufacturing history, from beginning to end, strongly determines how it behaves during combustion or detonation,” McClain said, according to the Purdue News website.
“We want to ensure that each step is catered toward the material and its intended use so that we’re getting a final product that functions in the way we expect.”
Traditionally, energetic materials are manufactured using processes focused on efficiency and scalability. However, these methods limit innovation and compromise optimal performance due to their large batch production. McClain and her research team focus on additive manufacturing or 3D printing of energetics, which gives researchers the freedom to experiment with properties such as “pore” defects, environmental conditions, and types of material.
In addition to her 3D printing research, McClain also explores how to improve traditional manufacturing methods. She has developed a patent-pending method for manufacturing a polymer-bonded explosive molding powder that is safer and more efficient in terms of time and waste.
McClain’s research is based at Purdue’s Maurice J. Zucrow Laboratories, the largest academic propulsion lab in the world. Funding for the project is provided by the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research’s Young Investigator Research program and the Army Research Office Energetic Materials Basic Research Center.
